title: Wiggs records Snoozer Quinn at the TB hospital
summary: Wiggs tells how he met Quinn through Peck Kelly, Quinn's style, and the difficult platter recording in the hospital that gave 12 sides.

blocks.x: there's a very, very interesting story behind Snoozer Quinn's rendition, and that was Snoozer's Wanderings. And I want Mr. Johnny Wiggs to tell us just how that record was recorded. Well, I hope we have time to start at the beginning. I met Snoozer when Peck Kelly sent for me. Peck Kelly was considered one of the greatest piano players that ever lived. And he was playing in Freeport, and they sent for me, and I pulled out my horn to play the dinner session. And it was a big band in those days. That was supposed to be the thing to have three brass and three reeds and the rest of the rhythm. And all of a sudden, Snoozer sat right next to me, and all of a sudden, I heard this guitar coming at me. And it was just too much to take. I just couldn't believe it, you know, because I'd heard Ed Lang previous to that, and I thought Ed Lang was the last word. Well, Snoozer was on the scene much to the surprise of the experts in the northern part of our United States. Snoozer was on the scene way before Ed Lang. And Snoozer was not influenced at all by Ed Lang. He was influenced of all things. I wrote an article about him, and I asked him who he was influenced by, fully expecting him to say Bick's butterback or Louis Armstrong. And lo and behold, he said Peck Kelly. I said, well, I didn't get Peck right away. He said, you know, it took me a year to find out what Peck was doing. And that's verified by some of the choruses that Jack Teagard plays, which were taken verbatim from Peck Kelly, and they're just perfectly exquisite. Anyway, Snoozer says he got his style from Peck Kelly. Now, to get to the recording, Victor had made eight sides and thrown them out because of Snoozer. I had thrown them out because they didn't think they were commercial. And Columbia, they were done in New Orleans. Columbia did the same thing in Houston, Texas, and threw them out because they didn't think they were commercial. So, and he played with Whiteman behind the rhythm boys, and you couldn't hear him at all, and he played with our fair governor, Jimmy Davis, and you couldn't hear him at all behind him. So I said, I got to get he was in the hospital with TB in any time, you know, it might happen. So I took my little platter recorder out there, and that was before this is so long ago. It was before the days of tape recorders. And I recorded him, thank God. And the good Lord was with me because the obstacles that I had to overcome were unbelievable. I had to run the recording machine. I had to play along, as you'll see pretty soon, with him. I had to

slam the door in nurses' faces. It was done out at the hospital, the TB hospital out the lake. I had to slam the door in audits' faces. I had to take phones off of hooks and brush off the hair which is caused by these platter machines. And lo and behold, if we didn't get 12 of fairly good sides, which are on the market now. Okay, and we're going to be hearing some of those, but first we have to bring you this message. Hi, Karate, after Shaven. Cologne presents. All right, we want to wish a very happy birthday this morning to Joey Catalinato, who is seven and having a birthday party, which we are going to this afternoon.
